F8.claim: the report's authors (Luke O’Brien, Deepa Kylasam Iyer, Johnnie Kallas) and date (2026)
F8.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F9.quote: A special thanks goes to the Cornell University ILR School and the University of Illinois LER School for funding our project
F9.lineage: operator: Cornell ILR and Illinois LER
F9.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F10.quote: Since funding cuts by the Reagan administration in the early-1980s, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) has only documented work stoppages involving 1,000 or more workers that last at least an entire shift.
F10.claim: since Reagan-era funding cuts in the early 1980s the BLS documents only stoppages of 1,000 or more workers lasting at least a full shift
F10.lineage: against the official count: the BLS threshold
F10.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F11.quote: By only recording large work stoppages, official data sources exclude the vast majority of strike activity, posing issues for policymakers, practitioners, and scholars in determining the extent of workplace conflict across the country.
F11.claim: official data exclude most strike activity, which leaves the extent of workplace conflict undetermined
F11.lineage: against the official count: the BLS threshold
F11.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F12.quote: In this report, we follow the lead of the BLS and document work stoppages, which include both strikes and lockouts.
F12.claim: the report documents work stoppages, strikes and lockouts, following the BLS
F12.lineage: what it counts: strikes, lockouts and labor protests
F12.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F13.quote: We generate all our data on strikes from several public sources, including existing work stoppage databases, news articles, and social media posts.
F13.claim: strike data from public sources: existing stoppage databases, news articles, social media posts
F13.lineage: method: public sources, verified and entered by hand
F13.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F14.quote: We follow rigorous verification protocols to ensure that a strike did in fact occur and to collect data on several related variables, including, but not limited to, the size, duration, industry, and demands of a strike.
F14.claim: verification protocols that a strike occurred; variables of size, duration, industry, demands
F14.lineage: method: public sources, verified and entered by hand
F14.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F15.quote: We link to the sources used to generate data on each strike on our site’s interactive map.
F15.claim: each strike's sources linked on the interactive map
F15.lineage: method: public sources, verified and entered by hand
F15.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F16.quote: We also collect data on labor protests but only provide summaries of work stoppages in this report because our count of protests is less comprehensive.
F16.claim: protests collected, but only stoppages summarized, the protest count being less comprehensive
F16.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F17.quote: In light of our rigorous protocols, we may underestimate total work stoppages as we cannot include events that do not have adequate verifiable information.
F17.claim: may underestimate stoppages, excluding events without adequate verifiable information
F17.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F18.quote: We added nine additional strikes to our 2024 data, which now includes 368 work stoppages.
F18.claim: 2024 revised upward by nine strikes, to 368 stoppages
F18.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F19.quote: We documented 303 work stoppages (298 strikes and five lockouts) involving approximately 290,000 workers. These work stoppages resulted in approximately 4,150,000 strike days.
F19.claim: 2025: 303 stoppages (298 strikes, five lockouts), about 290,000 workers, about 4,150,000 strike days
F19.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F20.quote: Despite a decline in the number of work stoppages in the Accommodation and Food Service sector, which tend to be relatively short and small in nature, more strikes occurred in this industry than any other.
F20.claim: Accommodation and Food Service had more strikes than any other industry
F20.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F21.quote: Another notable change came from the Healthcare and Social Assistance industry, which overtook Manufacturing and Educational Services to become the second largest industry by number of work stoppages. Healthcare and Social Assistance was also the largest industry by number of workers and strike days.
F21.claim: Healthcare and Social Assistance second by stoppages, first by workers and strike days
F21.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F22.quote: The demand for a first contract increased considerably between 2024 and 2025, going from 45 to 70, indicating ongoing activism by workers fighting for a first contract.
F22.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F23.quote: the West region accounted for 77.1% of all workers on strike in 2025, primarily due to labor activism in California.
F23.claim: the West held 77.1% of workers on strike in 2025
F23.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F24.quote: Finally, the share of strikes organized by nonunion workers reached the lowest levels since we began tracking work stoppages in 2021. Nonunion workers organized approximately 27.6% of all strikes between 2021-2024, including over 30% in 2021 and 2022, but just 18.5% in 2025.
F24.claim: the nonunion share of strikes fell to 18.5% in 2025, from about 27.6% over 2021–2024
F24.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F25.quote: Despite 36% of work stoppages involving fewer than 50 people, strikes that involved 1,000 or more workers represented 87% of all workers on strike in 2025.
F25.claim: 36% of stoppages under 50 people; strikes of 1,000 or more workers 87% of all strikers
F25.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')

F26.quote: A vast majority of all unionized strikes (95.5%) were authorized by a union, compared to 2.9% that were unauthorized and 1.7% that were unknown.
F26.claim: 95.5% of unionized strikes authorized by a union, 2.9% unauthorized, 1.7% unknown
F26.date: 2026 (the report's suggested citation: 'O’Brien, L., Iyer, D. K., and Kallas, J. (2026).')
